claim: Ruby et al. analyzed historical lifespan data on more than 3200 naked mole-rats, collected over a total observation period of about 38 years.
source: Ruby et al. recently analyzed historical lifespan data on more than 3200 naked mole-rats, collected over a total observation period of about 38 years (Ruby et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Ruby et al., 2018 as the source of this information.

claim: Ruby et al. report that mortality hazards do not seem to increase across the full range of naked mole-rats' so-far-observed lifespan.
source: They report that mortality hazards do not seem to increase across the full range of their so-far-observed lifespan, and conclude that this defiance of Gompertz's law 'uniquely identifies the naked mole-rat as a non-aging mammal'.
evidence: The claim references the findings reported by Ruby et al.

claim: Ruby et al. conclude that naked mole-rats' defiance of Gompertz's law 'uniquely identifies the naked mole-rat as a non-aging mammal'.
source: They report that mortality hazards do not seem to increase across the full range of their so-far-observed lifespan, and conclude that this defiance of Gompertz's law 'uniquely identifies the naked mole-rat as a non-aging mammal'.
evidence: The claim cites the conclusion from Ruby et al.

claim: The historical data set analyzed by Ruby et al. (2018) is strongly skewed toward animals born in 2008 or later.
source: The historical data set analyzed by Ruby et al. (2018) is strongly skewed toward animals born in 2008 or later (Figure 1)
evidence: The claim references Figure 1 which shows the distribution of birth years in the dataset.

claim: 87% of the animals in the Ruby et al. dataset have an observation time no longer than 8 years.
source: thus, the observation time for most (87%) of the animals is no longer than 8 years.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the dataset composition shown in Figure 1.

claim: The skew in the Ruby et al. dataset was caused by a massive expansion of the colony after 2007.
source: The reason for this skew – a massive expansion of the colony after 2007 – has been diligently explained by Ruby et al.
evidence: The claim cites Ruby et al. as the source of this explanation.

claim: Eight years correspond to approximately 25% of the maximum lifespan of naked mole-rats as recorded to date (>33 years).
source: Eight years correspond to approximately 25% of the maximum lifespan of the species as recorded to date (>33 years).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical calculation from known maximum lifespan data.

claim: Demographic aging (increasing mortality rates) is not expected to occur in young age cohorts of naked mole-rats.
source: In these young age cohorts, demographic aging (increasing mortality rates) is not expected to occur
evidence: The claim is based on general principles of aging biology and references to Ruby et al. and Jones et al., 2014.

claim: Gompertz mortality acceleration typically has its onset in the second half of the potential lifespan of a mammalian species.
source: as Ruby et al. correctly point out, Gompertz mortality acceleration typically has its onset in the second half of the potential lifespan of a mammalian species (see also Jones et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites Ruby et al. and Jones et al., 2014 as sources.

claim: If naked mole-rats were typical mammals, mortality acceleration would be expected to become apparent no earlier than at approximately 17 years (~50% of their maximum lifespan).
source: If naked mole-rats were typical mammals, one would expect mortality acceleration to become apparent no earlier than at approximately 17 years (~50% of their maximum lifespan as determined to date)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from general mammalian aging patterns applied to naked mole-rat lifespan data.

claim: Only 23 individuals (fewer than 1%) were observed for 18 years or longer in the most stringent analysis by Ruby et al.
source: However, only 23 individuals (i.e. fewer than 1%) were observed for 18 years or longer in the most stringent analysis by Ruby et al. (their Figure 1), and all of them were subsequently right-censored.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the data presented in Ruby et al.'s Figure 1.

claim: All 23 individuals observed for 18 years or longer in Ruby et al.'s most stringent analysis were subsequently right-censored.
source: However, only 23 individuals (i.e. fewer than 1%) were observed for 18 years or longer in the most stringent analysis by Ruby et al. (their Figure 1), and all of them were subsequently right-censored.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the data presented in Ruby et al.'s Figure 1.

claim: Ruby et al. limit their conclusions to the first 18 years in some passages of their manuscript.
source: Consequently, Ruby et al. limit their conclusions to the first 18 years in some passages ('The mortality hazard of naked mole-rats failed to increase for at least 18 years')
evidence: The claim directly quotes Ruby et al.'s manuscript.

claim: Ruby et al. limit their conclusions to the first 12 years in other passages of their manuscript.
source: or the first 12 years in other passages ('Our analyses […] confidently revealed a lack of demographic aging up to at least 4400 days of life (~12 years).').
evidence: The claim directly quotes Ruby et al.'s manuscript.

claim: Ruby et al. calculated one single hazard estimate for the entire final age group (>18 years) because of the small number of data points for mole-rats older than 18 years.
source: Because of the small number of data points for mole-rats older than 18 years, Ruby et al. calculated one single hazard estimate for the entire final age group (>18 years).
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach used by Ruby et al.

claim: The hazard estimate for the >18 years age group was not higher than the hazard estimates for the preceding age groups in Ruby et al.'s analysis.
source: The fact that this hazard estimate was not higher than the hazard estimates for the preceding age groups is surely a strong argument for the interpretation put forward by Ruby et al.
evidence: The claim describes a finding from Ruby et al.'s analysis.

claim: The question of whether mortality hazards increase toward the end of the >18 years age group must remain unanswered by Ruby et al.'s approach.
source: However, the decisive question of whether mortality hazards increase toward the end of that age group or not must, by definition, remain unanswered by this approach.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of the analytical method used.

claim: There is a decrease in survival at approximately 29 years in Figure 2A of Ruby et al.
source: Considering also the decrease in survival at approximately 29 years in Figure 2A of Ruby et al.
evidence: The claim references a specific observation from Ruby et al.'s Figure 2A.

claim: For the observation period of July 2, 1978, through January 30, 2008 (nearly 30 years, ~76% of the entire observation period), no deaths were reported in the Ruby et al. dataset.
source: Working with the raw data of Ruby et al. revealed that for the observation period of July 2, 1978, through January 30, 2008, that is for nearly 30 years (~76% of the entire observation period), no deaths were reported.
evidence: The claim is based on direct analysis of the raw data from Ruby et al.

claim: Only animals that had survived after January 30, 2008, and those born after that date were included in the Ruby et al. study.
source: They responded that indeed only animals that had survived after January 30, 2008, and those born after that date were included in the study.
evidence: The claim is based on personal communication from Ruby et al.

claim: Ruby et al. performed additional (unpublished) left-censorship-analysis to control for the missing death records between 1978 and 2008.
source: They further argued that additional (unpublished) left-censorship-analysis performed by them had satisfactorily controlled for the missing death records between 1978 and 2008
evidence: The claim is based on personal communication from Ruby et al.

claim: Ruby et al.'s conclusion about non-increasing hazard was not modified by their alternative left-censorship analytical approach.
source: and that their conclusion about non-increasing hazard had not been modified by this alternative analytical approach (Ruby et al., personal communication).
evidence: The claim is based on personal communication from Ruby et al.

claim: Ruby et al. list 250 animals which could not be included in the study due to insufficient resolution in their supplemental data.
source: In their supplemental data, Ruby et al. list 250 animals which could not be included in the study due to insufficient resolution (amongst them 37 animals labelled 'death date unknown')
evidence: The claim references data from Ruby et al.'s supplemental materials.

claim: Among the 250 excluded animals in Ruby et al.'s supplemental data, 37 animals were labelled 'death date unknown'.
source: In their supplemental data, Ruby et al. list 250 animals which could not be included in the study due to insufficient resolution (amongst them 37 animals labelled 'death date unknown')
evidence: The claim references specific data from Ruby et al.'s supplemental materials.

claim: Selective reporting of death data can bias all relevant hazard and Kaplan–Meier estimates (underestimation of hazard rates, overestimation of median survival).
source: In our view, these aspects need to be addressed because selective reporting of death data can clearly bias all relevant hazard and Kaplan–Meier estimates (underestimation of hazard rates, overestimation of median survival).
evidence: The claim is based on established statistical knowledge about survival analysis.

claim: No deaths occurring later than 6529 days (~18 years) are recorded in the most stringent analysis by Ruby et al. (their Figure 1A).
source: Since death events at ages up to 29 years may be missing, while no deaths occurring later than 6529 days (~18 years) are recorded in the most stringent analysis by Ruby et al. (their Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of data presented in Ruby et al.'s Figure 1A.

claim: In a simulation using Fukomys mole-rat data, removing death data over the first 75% of the observation period decreased the slope of the survival curve.
source: Not surprisingly, the slope of the survival curve decreases, median survival increases by more than 30%, and the estimated constant mortality hazard per day decreases by more than 25%, from 2.6 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3A) to 1.9 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the authors' simulation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In a simulation using Fukomys mole-rat data, removing death data over the first 75% of the observation period increased median survival by more than 30%.
source: Not surprisingly, the slope of the survival curve decreases, median survival increases by more than 30%, and the estimated constant mortality hazard per day decreases by more than 25%, from 2.6 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3A) to 1.9 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the authors' simulation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In a simulation using Fukomys mole-rat data, removing death data over the first 75% of the observation period decreased the estimated constant mortality hazard per day by more than 25%, from 2.6 × 10−4 per day to 1.9 × 10−4 per day.
source: Not surprisingly, the slope of the survival curve decreases, median survival increases by more than 30%, and the estimated constant mortality hazard per day decreases by more than 25%, from 2.6 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3A) to 1.9 × 10−4 per day (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the authors' simulation shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ruby et al. (2018) report a consistent estimate for mortality hazard of 8 × 10−5 per day for the naked mole-rat.
source: Although this is just a single example and both data sets may quantitatively react differently to the introduced bias, these results indicate that the 'consistent estimate for mortality hazard (8 × 10−5 per day)' for the naked mole-rat (Ruby et al., 2018) is probably underestimated.
evidence: The claim cites a specific finding from Ruby et al., 2018.

claim: The consistent estimate for mortality hazard (8 × 10−5 per day) for the naked mole-rat reported by Ruby et al. (2018) is probably underestimated.
source: Although this is just a single example and both data sets may quantitatively react differently to the introduced bias, these results indicate that the 'consistent estimate for mortality hazard (8 × 10−5 per day)' for the naked mole-rat (Ruby et al., 2018) is probably underestimated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation results showing bias effects.

claim: Figure 3 of Ruby et al. shows for the first time that, under laboratory conditions, naked mole-rat breeders appear to live longer than helpers.
source: Of note, we believe that Figure 3 of Ruby et al. contains an important finding because it shows for the first time that, under laboratory conditions, naked mole-rat breeders appear to live longer than helpers.
evidence: The claim references a finding from Ruby et al.'s Figure 3.

claim: Data from the wild previously suggested a difference in life expectancy between breeders and helpers for naked mole-rats.
source: Until recently, only data from the wild suggested this difference in life expectancy for naked mole-rats (Braude, 1991; Buffenstein, 2008).
evidence: The claim cites Braude, 1991 and Buffenstein, 2008 as sources.

claim: Several Fukomys species show divergent survival trajectories of breeders and non-breeders.
source: If corroborated by a stricter, unbiased analysis, this pattern would show a striking similarity to the divergent survival trajectories of breeders and non-breeders in several Fukomys species (Dammann and Burda, 2006; Dammann et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim cites multiple studies (Dammann and Burda, 2006; Dammann et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2013) as sources.

claim: Many if not all social mole-rat species may have evolved life-prolonging mechanisms associated with sexual activity, breeding, or both.
source: and thus would support the hypothesis that many if not all social mole-rat species may have evolved life-prolonging mechanisms associated with sexual activity, breeding, or both, despite the classic trade-off between reproduction and somatic maintenance.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by inference from the cited data.

claim: There is a classic trade-off between reproduction and somatic maintenance.
source: and thus would support the hypothesis that many if not all social mole-rat species may have evolved life-prolonging mechanisms associated with sexual activity, breeding, or both, despite the classic trade-off between reproduction and somatic maintenance.
evidence: The claim references established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: Naked mole-rats may age after defying the Gompertz–Makeham timeline over large portions of their documented lifespan.
source: Even if naked mole-rats defy the Gompertz–Makeham timeline over large portions of their documented lifespan, they may nonetheless age afterwards
evidence: The claim is presented as a possibility based on speculation and references to Edrey et al., 2011.

claim: Edrey et al., 2011 found signs of age-associated pathologies in naked mole-rats older than 28 years.
source: (see, for example, Edrey et al., 2011 for signs of age-associated pathologies in naked mole-rats older than 28 years).
evidence: The claim cites Edrey et al., 2011 as the source.

claim: The scientific literature describes a number of aging phenotypes for naked mole-rats.
source: In fact, the scientific literature regarding naked mole-rats describes a number of aging phenotypes for these mammals (see Edrey et al., 2011; Beltrán-Sánchez and Finch, 2018; Finch, 2009; Heinze et al., 2018 and references therein)
evidence: The claim cites multiple sources (Edrey et al., 2011; Beltrán-Sánchez and Finch, 2018; Finch, 2009; Heinze et al., 2018).

claim: The lifespan data of Ruby et al. (2018) are skewed and biased.
source: In summary, we argue that the lifespan data of Ruby et al. (2018) have to be used and interpreted with caution because they are skewed and biased.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of the dataset structure and missing data.

claim: The maximum lifespan of naked mole-rats as recorded to date is more than 33 years.
source: Eight years correspond to approximately 25% of the maximum lifespan of the species as recorded to date (>33 years).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about naked mole-rat longevity records.

claim: The observation period in the Ruby et al. dataset spans approximately 38 years.
source: Working with the raw data of Ruby et al. revealed that for the observation period of July 2, 1978, through January 30, 2008, that is for nearly 30 years (~76% of the entire observation period), no deaths were reported.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the stated 76% representing nearly 30 years.

claim: The Kaplan-Meier survival curve for Fukomys anselli and Fukomys anselli x kafuensis shows a median survival after 0.5 years of 7.99 years (95% CI, 7.04–9.60 years) with original unbiased data.
source: (A) Original data from 339 animals; median survival after 0.5 years, 7.99 years (95% CI, 7.04–9.60 years).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Kaplan-Meier survival curve for Fukomys anselli and Fukomys anselli x kafuensis shows a median survival after 0.5 years of 10.80 years (95% CI, 8.82–11.39 years) when animals that died before 2010 are artificially deleted from the dataset.
source: (B) Biased data presentation: animals that died before 2010 have been (artificially) deleted from the dataset. Median survival after 0.5 years, 10.80 years (95% CI, 8.82–11.39 years).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The original Fukomys dataset contained 339 animals.
source: (A) Original data from 339 animals; median survival after 0.5 years, 7.99 years (95% CI, 7.04–9.60 years).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Figure 2 caption.

claim: The authors' simulation removed death data from the first 75% (1984–2010) of the total observation period (1984–2018) in the Fukomys dataset.
source: We tried to exemplify the potential bias by modeling own lifespan data for related Fukomys mole-rats (Figure 2A) and using this dataset to 'simulate' the loss of death data over the first 75% (1984–2010) of the total observation period (1984–2018).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology of the simulation performed by the authors.
